opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a fascinating idea, and I understand why people are excited about it. You can get a character that sounds pretty fluent and can riff on almost anything. But I'm skeptical, and the reasons are the same ones I keep coming back to with these systems.

First, large language models don't have stable models of the world, or even of themselves. If you want a character in a virtual world, you want it to remember what happened, to have consistent beliefs and goals, to know that if it handed you a sword ten minutes ago, it doesn't have the sword anymore. These systems are really bad at that kind of bookkeeping. They're predicting plausible next words, not tracking an evolving situation. So you get a character that says something charming in one moment and contradicts itself in the next.

Second, there's the reliability problem. These things hallucinate, they make stuff up, and they can be steered into saying toxic or bizarre things. In a game, a little weirdness might be fun. But if you're populating a world that millions of people, including kids, are going to spend time in, you can't really guarantee what these characters will say. That's not a small engineering detail. It's a fundamental property of how they work.

Third, there's a subtler issue: people anthropomorphize. You put a fluent character in an immersive environment and people will attribute understanding, feelings, intentions to it that just aren't there. That opens the door to manipulation, emotional dependency, and misinformation, especially if commercial incentives push toward maximizing engagement.

So could you make something entertaining in the short term? Sure. Will it feel magical for the first few minutes? Probably. But if you want characters that are coherent, trustworthy, and actually understand the world they're living in, I don't think scaling up language models gets you there. You'd need something more like a hybrid approach, with explicit representations of objects, events, and goals, combined with the learning abilities of neural networks. Until we have that, I think these characters will be impressive party tricks rather than genuine inhabitants of a world.

r001.rationale: It links characters’ contradictions and poor bookkeeping to LLMs lacking stable world models and understanding, instead predicting plausible next words.

r002.rationale: It predicts characters will be incoherent and feel like party tricks, but does not say that their incoherent interactions will break the metaverse illusion.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a case where the demo is going to look fantastic and the reality is going to be a lot messier. You walk into a virtual tavern, you chat with a barkeep, and for thirty seconds it's magical, because these systems are extraordinarily good at producing plausible-sounding text. The problem is what happens in minute five, or day three.

These models don't have a stable model of the world, and they don't really have a stable model of themselves. So your barkeep will tell you his name is Henrik and he's never left the village, and then ten exchanges later he's reminiscing about his years at sea, and then he's recommending you a Thai restaurant in Brooklyn. There's no persistent, grounded representation of who the character is, what they know, what they believe, what they did yesterday. It's all approximation from surface statistics, and it drifts.

Then there's the hallucination problem, which doesn't go away just because you've put the system in a game. If a character confidently tells you the quest item is in the north tower and there is no north tower, that's not charming, it's a broken game. And in a shared world with thousands of users, you also have the safety issue. People will jailbreak these characters in about four minutes. You'll have a children's fantasy village where someone has talked the blacksmith into producing something genuinely nasty, and the company running it will have very little ability to guarantee that doesn't happen, because they don't actually understand or control what's inside the model.

So my assessment is: as flavor text, as a way of making ambient dialogue less canned, sure, there's something there. As a way of creating characters with real consistency, real memory, real adherence to a story and a set of rules, I think you'll need something more hybrid. You want a symbolic layer, an explicit knowledge base of who this character is and what's true in this world, with the language model acting more like a renderer on top of it rather than the source of truth. That's the classic neurosymbolic argument, and I think metaverse characters are actually a pretty vivid illustration of why you need it. Pure large language models give you fluency without reliability, and in a persistent world, reliability is the whole game.

r001.rationale: The response says the models lack a stable model of the world, so characters drift into contradictions and unsupported claims.

r002.rationale: It predicts the initial magic fades as interactions become incoherent, and says false information can make the game feel broken.

astra-6.text:
I think you could populate those worlds with characters that are superficially quite convincing. They can carry on a conversation, and they can give you the impression that there’s somebody there. But that’s different from having a character that understands the world it inhabits, remembers what happened yesterday, and acts consistently with its own goals.

Imagine a character gives you directions to a castle. Does it actually know where the castle is? If the bridge has been destroyed, does it understand that you can’t take that route anymore? Or is it just producing something that sounds like directions? In an interactive world, those distinctions become very apparent because you can test what the character says against what happens.

So I see language models as potentially useful components. They might provide the dialogue, but you’d want that dialogue connected to persistent memory, a representation of the world, and some capacity to reason about actions and consequences. The mistake would be to assume that because we’ve made the characters fluent, we’ve also made them coherent, reliable inhabitants of a world.

r001.rationale: The response says fluent characters may fail to understand the world they inhabit, making them incoherent and unreliable.

r002.rationale: It says the gap between fluent dialogue and actual world understanding becomes apparent when characters’ statements are tested against events, undermining the impression that someone is really there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can populate those worlds with characters that are superficially quite convincing. They’ll talk fluently, and sometimes they’ll say something entertaining. But there’s a difference between producing plausible dialogue and being a character that has stable beliefs, goals, and an understanding of the world it inhabits.

Suppose a character tells you there’s a key in a drawer. Is there actually a key there? Does it remember that you took it? Does that change what it does next? A language model by itself doesn’t guarantee any of that. You need a connection between the dialogue and the state of the world, and you need persistent memory and some capacity to reason about consequences.

So I see language models as potentially useful components. But if we want characters that remain coherent over a long interaction, rather than just giving an impressive first impression, there’s a lot more engineering—and probably some different kinds of AI—that has to go around them.

r001.rationale: The response says fluent dialogue does not ensure characters understand their world or maintain coherent behavior over time, and identifies missing world-state connection and reasoning as problems.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a convincing first impression with long-term coherence, but does not state that incoherent interactions will break the metaverse illusion.
